extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century London readers interested in manners, theatre, fashion, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A Tatler-periodical essay offering prescriptive commentary on social conduct, conversation, courtship, theatrical writing, and acting, with examples and anecdotes drawn from contemporary London life and the stage. The page mixes moral guidance, theatrical criticism, and satirical sketches aimed at improving or exposing social behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman / man of conversation — essential qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is generally thought, that warmth of imagination, quick relish of pleasure, and a manner of becoming it, are the most essential qualities for forming this sort of man... the height of good breeding is shown rather in never giving offence, than in doing obliging things... The most necessary talent therefore in a man of conversation... is a good judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Sophronius: good judgment lets him "be master of his companion, without letting him see it," act with ease among men of pleasure and business, deny unwanted requests convincingly, keep equality in society by helping and being helped, avoid appearing cunning, and combine discretion with cheerfulness. Use these traits to evaluate or cultivate a man of conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretty Fellow — artificial mimicry as an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: "In imitation of this agreeable being, is made that animal we call a Pretty Fellow... makes his own an artificial one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anti-pattern (Jack Dimple) is shown by constant self-admiration and affectation (e.g., frequent mirror-checking, rehearsed airs). Evaluate such figures as superficial: they mimic natural behaviour rather than possess it. Avoid theatrical self-fashioning that substitutes artifice for genuine good-breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful courtship (ogling) — eye-language and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is nothing but ogling with skill carries a woman... This requires an exquisite judgment, to take the language of her eyes to yours exactly, and not let yours talk too fast for hers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courtship depends on subtle, well-timed glances and reciprocal signals rather than clumsy forwardness. Examples: Beau Frisk's bench-at-the-play scenario and the 'watchful glance' that solicits a second twinkle. Advice: match pace and intensity, do not rush, treat attentive following as pleasurable rather than servile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playwriting — use dress/habit to signal character
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is no difficulty to get hats, and swords, and wigs... and make a man show himself by his habit... and not be obliged to make those characters talk in different dialects to be distinguished from each other. This is certainly the surest and best way of writing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern playwrights can rely on costume and outward habit to indicate rank/role so that dialectal or manner-of-speaking differences are less necessary. This is offered as practical guidance for efficient contemporary writing and staging: distinct visual cues reduce the need for exaggerated verbal differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playwriting — distinctiveness of sentiment per character
rubrics_metrics.description: "No one sentence in a play should be spoken by any one character, which could possibly enter into the head of any other man represented in it; but every sentiment should be peculiar to him only who utters it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters ought to have unique voices and motives so their speeches are believable as arising from their individual psychology and situation. The essay notes Ben Jonson's skill in keeping characters' discourses 'skilfully apart' even when driven by the same passion (e.g., money). It also warns that enforcing absolute uniqueness could shorten many modern plays, so apply the rule judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting — naturalness and restraint; avoid overacting
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nature excellently represented in his manner of action; in which he ever avoided that general fault in players, of doing too much."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for Cave Underhill as exemplifying natural, restrained comic acting. The guidance is to favor representations of 'still-life' or restraint over exaggerated theatricality; overacting is identified as a common fault. Evaluate actors on their ability to convey character with economy and truth rather than excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors should not add to the author's text (onstage authorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is certainly nature excellently represented in his manner of action; in which he ever avoided that general fault in players, of doing too much. It must be confessed, he has not the merit of some ingenious persons now on the stage, of adding to his authors..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast is drawn between past actors (who 'went out of the world, without having ever spoke one word of their own') and modern players who add lines or embellish authors' works. The implicit criterion: actors should respect the author's text and avoid unauthorized additions that alter the playwright's intention.
